Q0174

“Those who in ancient or modern times achieved great enterprises and profound…” — Wang Guowei (Remarks on Lyrics in the Human…)

Verified English quotation. Primary source: Remarks on Lyrics in the Human World, §26. Theme: learning.

Quotes / Wang Guowei / Q0174

English

Those who in ancient or modern times achieved great enterprises and profound learning must pass through three realms: first, standing alone atop a high tower after the west wind withers the green trees, gazing to the end of the road at heaven's edge; second, the belt growing looser without regret, wasting away for the beloved; third, searching a thousand times in the crowd, then suddenly turning — and finding that person standing where the lanterns grow sparse.
Thinker Wang Guowei
School Modern Chinese Thought
Source Remarks on Lyrics in the Human World, §26
Theme Learning
Another quotation More from this thinker

Source and attribution

The archive attributes this English wording to Remarks on Lyrics in the Human World, §26 and files it under Modern Chinese Thought. That locator distinguishes the passage from loose internet attributions: readers can return to the named work or section to check translation, surrounding argument, and edition-specific wording.

About Wang Guowei

Wang Guowei (1877–1927) was a late Qing–Republican scholar who joined classical Chinese learning with Western aesthetics and philosophy. He wrote on tragedy, ci poetry, oracle bones, and the history of Song–Yuan drama.

How to read this passage

Education is not only information transfer; it is the shaping of attention and character. Confucian learning, Socratic midwifery, and Deweyan growth offer rival models. This passage enters that discussion through learning, perseverance.

Concepts in this quote

Learning
Learning is philosophy’s practical twin: how judgment is formed through study, error, dialogue, and habit.
Perseverance
Perseverance appears in this archive as a live philosophical concern—not a slogan. These verified English passages show how thinkers treat perseverance as a problem of judgment, practice, or explanation.
